demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Mereana had been 46 when she lost her younger brother in a sudden, violent car crash on a wet evening outside Auckland, a death so unexpected that the first call from the hospital felt to her like a mistake. She remembered the event now in fragments rather than as a continuous story: the blue glare of emergency lights on the rain-slick road, the sound of a voice on the phone saying her brother’s name in a careful, practised tone, the sight of her own hands gripping the kitchen counter until her knuckles went white. Even years later, when she tried to recall that night, the memory came back in a few fixed pictures, as if the scene had been cut into separate still frames that she could not make join together. At other times, the recollection arrived with an almost physical force. She would be at her desk at the forensic lab, logging evidence or reviewing reports, and a detail from that night would come back so sharply that she had to stop what she was doing. What disturbed her most was that she could hear parts of it in her head exactly as though they were happening again: the clipped tone of the call, the muffled background noise, the words she wished she could unhear. When that happened, she became overwhelmed by emotion so quickly that she had to put her pen down, stare at the paperwork without seeing it, and wait for the wave to pass before she could continue.

In the weeks after the death, Mereana found herself moving through her days as though the ground beneath them had changed shape. She had always been a careful, steady worker, but returning to the forensic unit became increasingly difficult. The sight of case files, official calls, and the quiet concentration of the office could all bring her back to the night she was told her brother had died. She began to go to work as late as she could manage and sometimes delayed leaving home altogether, sitting in the car outside the lab for several minutes before going in. On the hardest mornings she had taken sick leave or simply found reasons to stay away, telling herself she needed a day to recover, then another. At home, her evenings became stretched and unsettled. Rather than going to bed at a normal hour, she stayed up until very late, scrolling mindlessly or sitting in silence after her husband had gone to sleep, unwilling to let the house become quiet in the way it was that night. She also started to restrict food, not because she believed it would solve anything, but because eating felt difficult when her chest was tight with grief and the memory of that call sat in the room with her. Over time, these habits shaped the rhythm of her life, leaving her tired, withdrawn, and less present both at work and at home.

What had changed most profoundly was the way Mereana understood her future. She had come to believe that something essential had been taken from her when her brother died, not only the person himself but her sense that life was orderly, reliable, or worthy of trust. She spoke with a flat certainty that she had lost her faith in people, life, and in any higher power that might have been listening that night. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore, and she described her world as if the event had broken it beyond repair. In her mind, the trauma had not simply happened within her life; it had destroyed it. This conviction showed itself in the way she spoke about ordinary things. Work, which had once given her a clear role and a sense of usefulness, now felt oddly detached from purpose. Family dinners with her husband were quieter than before, and she often withdrew into herself rather than joining the conversation. She could appear composed to others, but she lived with the private sense that the structure around her had been shattered permanently.

By the time she sought help, it was because the pattern had become impossible to ignore. Mereana was exhausted from the late nights, increasingly isolated by her avoidance of work, and alarmed by how quickly the memory could seize her in the middle of a normal day. She said she was not sure she could keep functioning if things remained as they were, and what frightened her most was not another image or another call, but the thought that she might continue living in a life that felt emptied of meaning. At the same time, she admitted to hoping that therapy might help her bear the memories without having to stop everything, and perhaps allow her to believe again that her life had not been wholly destroyed.
